claim: Extensive fibrin deposition occurs in the lungs of COVID-19 patients.
source: Extensive fibrin deposition in the lungs and altered levels of circulating blood coagulation proteins in COVID-19 patients imply local derangement of pathways that limit fibrin formation and/or promote its clearance.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established observation about COVID-19 patients.

claim: COVID-19 patients have altered levels of circulating blood coagulation proteins.
source: Extensive fibrin deposition in the lungs and altered levels of circulating blood coagulation proteins in COVID-19 patients imply local derangement of pathways that limit fibrin formation and/or promote its clearance.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established observation about COVID-19 patients.

claim: mRNA levels for C1-inhibitor are significantly reduced in COVID-19 patients.
source: mRNA levels for regulators of the kallikrein–kinin (C1-inhibitor), coagulation (thrombomodulin, endothelial protein C receptor), and fibrinolytic (urokinase and urokinase receptor) pathways were significantly reduced in COVID-19 patients.
evidence: This is a direct finding from the transcriptional analysis presented in the study.

claim: mRNA levels for thrombomodulin are significantly reduced in COVID-19 patients.
source: mRNA levels for regulators of the kallikrein–kinin (C1-inhibitor), coagulation (thrombomodulin, endothelial protein C receptor), and fibrinolytic (urokinase and urokinase receptor) pathways were significantly reduced in COVID-19 patients.
evidence: This is a direct finding from the transcriptional analysis presented in the study.

claim: mRNA levels for endothelial protein C receptor are significantly reduced in COVID-19 patients.
source: mRNA levels for regulators of the kallikrein–kinin (C1-inhibitor), coagulation (thrombomodulin, endothelial protein C receptor), and fibrinolytic (urokinase and urokinase receptor) pathways were significantly reduced in COVID-19 patients.
evidence: This is a direct finding from the transcriptional analysis presented in the study.

claim: mRNA levels for urokinase are significantly reduced in COVID-19 patients.
source: mRNA levels for regulators of the kallikrein–kinin (C1-inhibitor), coagulation (thrombomodulin, endothelial protein C receptor), and fibrinolytic (urokinase and urokinase receptor) pathways were significantly reduced in COVID-19 patients.
evidence: This is a direct finding from the transcriptional analysis presented in the study.

claim: mRNA levels for urokinase receptor are significantly reduced in COVID-19 patients.
source: mRNA levels for regulators of the kallikrein–kinin (C1-inhibitor), coagulation (thrombomodulin, endothelial protein C receptor), and fibrinolytic (urokinase and urokinase receptor) pathways were significantly reduced in COVID-19 patients.
evidence: This is a direct finding from the transcriptional analysis presented in the study.

claim: Transcripts for tissue factor were not increased in BALF from COVID-19 patients.
source: While transcripts for several coagulation proteins were increased, those encoding tissue factor, the protein that initiates coagulation and whose expression is frequently increased in inflammatory disorders, were not increased in BALF from COVID-19 patients.
evidence: This is a direct finding from the transcriptional analysis presented in the study.

claim: Tissue factor expression is frequently increased in inflammatory disorders.
source: While transcripts for several coagulation proteins were increased, those encoding tissue factor, the protein that initiates coagulation and whose expression is frequently increased in inflammatory disorders, were not increased in BALF from COVID-19 patients.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about tissue factor behavior in inflammatory conditions.

claim: Enhanced propagation of coagulation is a driver of coagulopathy in the lungs of COVID-19 patients.
source: Our analysis implicates enhanced propagation of coagulation and decreased fibrinolysis as drivers of the coagulopathy in the lungs of COVID-19 patients.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the transcriptional data analysis presented in the study.

claim: Decreased fibrinolysis is a driver of coagulopathy in the lungs of COVID-19 patients.
source: Our analysis implicates enhanced propagation of coagulation and decreased fibrinolysis as drivers of the coagulopathy in the lungs of COVID-19 patients.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the transcriptional data analysis presented in the study.

claim: The bradykinin storm model for COVID-19 pathogenesis was developed from analyses of gene expression, clinical, autopsy, pathology, and ChIP-Seq data.
source: The bradykinin storm model for COVID-19 pathogenesis was recently developed from our analyses of gene expression, clinical, autopsy, pathology, and ChIP-Seq data (Garvin et al., 2020).
evidence: This references prior work by the authors with a citation.

claim: Several clinical studies have demonstrated positive results from therapeutic interventions predicted by the bradykinin storm model.
source: Several clinical studies by other groups have demonstrated positive results from therapeutic interventions predicted by our model (Entrenas Castillo et al., 2020; van de Veerdonk et al., 2020; WHO Rapid Evidence Appraisal for COVID-19 Therapies (REACT) Working Group et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple clinical studies.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 displays considerable tissue tropism.
source: SARS-CoV-2 displays considerable tissue tropism (Adachi et al., 2020; Barton et al., 2020; Su et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: The time course for the development of severe COVID-19 disease is typically 8–12 days.
source: The time course for the development of severe disease is typically 8–12 days, but some patients rapidly deteriorate about 7 days following development of symptoms.
evidence: This is stated as established clinical knowledge about COVID-19 disease progression.

claim: Some COVID-19 patients rapidly deteriorate about 7 days following development of symptoms.
source: The time course for the development of severe disease is typically 8–12 days, but some patients rapidly deteriorate about 7 days following development of symptoms.
evidence: This is stated as established clinical knowledge about COVID-19 disease progression.

claim: Lung tissue from people who died from COVID-19 has pauci-inflammatory septal capillary injury.
source: Lung tissue from people who died from COVID-19 has pauci-inflammatory septal capillary injury and luminal and mural fibrin deposition in alveolar septal capillaries (Lax et al., 2020; Magro et al., 2020), thrombi in small- and medium-sized arteries (Lax et al., 2020; Magro et al., 2020), and fibrinous thrombi in small pulmonary arterioles with evidence of tumefaction of the endothelium (Dolhnikoff et al., 2020; Fox et al., 2020; Geerdes-Fenge et al., 2020; Lax et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to autopsy studies.

claim: Lung tissue from people who died from COVID-19 has luminal and mural fibrin deposition in alveolar septal capillaries.
source: Lung tissue from people who died from COVID-19 has pauci-inflammatory septal capillary injury and luminal and mural fibrin deposition in alveolar septal capillaries (Lax et al., 2020; Magro et al., 2020), thrombi in small- and medium-sized arteries (Lax et al., 2020; Magro et al., 2020), and fibrinous thrombi in small pulmonary arterioles with evidence of tumefaction of the endothelium (Dolhnikoff et al., 2020; Fox et al., 2020; Geerdes-Fenge et al., 2020; Lax et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to autopsy studies.

claim: Lung tissue from people who died from COVID-19 has thrombi in small- and medium-sized arteries.
source: Lung tissue from people who died from COVID-19 has pauci-inflammatory septal capillary injury and luminal and mural fibrin deposition in alveolar septal capillaries (Lax et al., 2020; Magro et al., 2020), thrombi in small- and medium-sized arteries (Lax et al., 2020; Magro et al., 2020), and fibrinous thrombi in small pulmonary arterioles with evidence of tumefaction of the endothelium (Dolhnikoff et al., 2020; Fox et al., 2020; Geerdes-Fenge et al., 2020; Lax et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to autopsy studies.

claim: Lung tissue from people who died from COVID-19 has fibrinous thrombi in small pulmonary arterioles with evidence of tumefaction of the endothelium.
source: Lung tissue from people who died from COVID-19 has pauci-inflammatory septal capillary injury and luminal and mural fibrin deposition in alveolar septal capillaries (Lax et al., 2020; Magro et al., 2020), thrombi in small- and medium-sized arteries (Lax et al., 2020; Magro et al., 2020), and fibrinous thrombi in small pulmonary arterioles with evidence of tumefaction of the endothelium (Dolhnikoff et al., 2020; Fox et al., 2020; Geerdes-Fenge et al., 2020; Lax et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to autopsy studies.

claim: Administering tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) to dissolve fibrin transiently alleviates respiratory distress in COVID-19 patients.
source: A report that administering tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) to dissolve fibrin transiently alleviates respiratory distress in COVID-19 patients supports the premise that fibrin deposition contributes to the respiratory failure (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a clinical report.

claim: Fibrin deposition contributes to respiratory failure in COVID-19.
source: A report that administering tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) to dissolve fibrin transiently alleviates respiratory distress in COVID-19 patients supports the premise that fibrin deposition contributes to the respiratory failure (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is inferred from the clinical observation that tPA alleviates respiratory distress, supported by citation.

claim: COVID-19 hypoxemia stems at least partially from fibrin deposits surrounding alveoli that restrict oxygen transfer.
source: Thus, it appears that COVID-19 hypoxemia stems at least partially from fibrin deposits surrounding alveoli that restrict oxygen transfer and microvascular thrombi that cause ventilation–perfusion defects.
evidence: This is inferred from the pathological findings and clinical observations discussed.

claim: COVID-19 hypoxemia stems at least partially from microvascular thrombi that cause ventilation–perfusion defects.
source: Thus, it appears that COVID-19 hypoxemia stems at least partially from fibrin deposits surrounding alveoli that restrict oxygen transfer and microvascular thrombi that cause ventilation–perfusion defects.
evidence: This is inferred from the pathological findings and clinical observations discussed.

claim: COVID-19 patients have increased levels of fibrinogen.
source: Changes include increased levels of coagulation proteins associated with the acute phase response (e.g., fibrinogen and factor VIII) and endothelial activation (e.g., von Willebrand factor), as well as elevated biomarkers of coagulation activation (e.g., D-dimer) (Chen et al., 2020; Gattinoni et al., 2020; Helms et al., 2020; Middeldorp et al., 2020; Panigada et al., 2020; Tang et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2020a; Helms et al., 2020; Middeldorp et al., 2020; Panigada et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to clinical studies.

claim: COVID-19 patients have increased levels of factor VIII.
source: Changes include increased levels of coagulation proteins associated with the acute phase response (e.g., fibrinogen and factor VIII) and endothelial activation (e.g., von Willebrand factor), as well as elevated biomarkers of coagulation activation (e.g., D-dimer) (Chen et al., 2020; Gattinoni et al., 2020; Helms et al., 2020; Middeldorp et al., 2020; Panigada et al., 2020; Tang et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2020a; Helms et al., 2020; Middeldorp et al., 2020; Panigada et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to clinical studies.

claim: COVID-19 patients have increased levels of von Willebrand factor.
source: Changes include increased levels of coagulation proteins associated with the acute phase response (e.g., fibrinogen and factor VIII) and endothelial activation (e.g., von Willebrand factor), as well as elevated biomarkers of coagulation activation (e.g., D-dimer) (Chen et al., 2020; Gattinoni et al., 2020; Helms et al., 2020; Middeldorp et al., 2020; Panigada et al., 2020; Tang et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2020a; Helms et al., 2020; Middeldorp et al., 2020; Panigada et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to clinical studies.

claim: COVID-19 patients have elevated D-dimer levels.
source: Changes include increased levels of coagulation proteins associated with the acute phase response (e.g., fibrinogen and factor VIII) and endothelial activation (e.g., von Willebrand factor), as well as elevated biomarkers of coagulation activation (e.g., D-dimer) (Chen et al., 2020; Gattinoni et al., 2020; Helms et al., 2020; Middeldorp et al., 2020; Panigada et al., 2020; Tang et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2020a; Helms et al., 2020; Middeldorp et al., 2020; Panigada et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to clinical studies.

claim: Thrombotic events have been detected in up to 30% of COVID-19 patients.
source: Accordingly, thrombotic events have been detected in up to 30% of COVID-19 patients (Helms et al., 2020; Middeldorp et al., 2020; Panigada et al., 2020) including large vessel occlusions such as deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, and ischemic stroke, as well as microvascular thrombosis and extravascular fibrin deposition in a variety of tissues including lung and skin (Helms et al., 2020; Middeldorp et al., 2020; Panigada et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: The plasma kallikrein–kinin system is comprised of factor XII, prekallikrein, and high-molecular-weight kininogen.
source: The plasma kallikrein–kinin system is comprised of the protease precursors factor XII (FXII, encoded by F12) and prekallikrein (encoded by KLKB1) and the cofactor high-molecular-weight kininogen (HK, encoded by KNG1) (Schmaier, 2016; Schmaier et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: FXII and prekallikrein undergo reciprocal activation to the proteases FXIIa and kallikrein in healthy individuals.
source: In healthy individuals, FXII and prekallikrein undergo reciprocal activation to the proteases FXIIa and kallikrein (Revenko et al., 2011; Schmaier, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Kallikrein cleaves HK to liberate bradykinin.
source: Kallikrein cleaves HK to liberate bradykinin, which contributes to setting vascular tone and permeability by interacting with bradykinin receptors (encoded by BDKRB1 and BDKRB2) (Marceau et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Bradykinin contributes to setting vascular tone and permeability by interacting with bradykinin receptors.
source: Kallikrein cleaves HK to liberate bradykinin, which contributes to setting vascular tone and permeability by interacting with bradykinin receptors (encoded by BDKRB1 and BDKRB2) (Marceau et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The kallikrein-kinin process is regulated by C1-Inhibitor.
source: This process is regulated by C1-Inhibitor (encoded by SERPING1) (Marceau et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Congenital C1-Inhibitor deficiency causes hereditary angioedema.
source: Congenital C1-Inhibitor deficiency causes hereditary angioedema, which is characterized by bouts of bradykinin-induced soft tissue swelling (Busse and Christiansen, 2020; Cicardi and Zuraw, 2018).
evidence: This is established medical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Hereditary angioedema is characterized by bouts of bradykinin-induced soft tissue swelling.
source: Congenital C1-Inhibitor deficiency causes hereditary angioedema, which is characterized by bouts of bradykinin-induced soft tissue swelling (Busse and Christiansen, 2020; Cicardi and Zuraw, 2018).
evidence: This is established medical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: C1-Inhibitor in blood is primarily of hepatocyte origin.
source: C1-Inhibitor in blood is primarily of hepatocyte origin, although it also is produced by other cell types including vascular endothelium (Prada et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: C1-Inhibitor is also produced by vascular endothelium.
source: C1-Inhibitor in blood is primarily of hepatocyte origin, although it also is produced by other cell types including vascular endothelium (Prada et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Transcripts encoding C1-Inhibitor were decreased 80-fold in BALF from COVID-19 patients.
source: Transcripts encoding C1-Inhibitor were decreased 80-fold in BALF from COVID-19 patients (Table 1), raising the possibilities that contact activation-initiated thrombin generation is locally dysregulated and control of bradykinin production is compromised.
evidence: This is a direct finding from the study's data analysis, with reference to Table 1.

claim: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) degrades bradykinin.
source: Furthermore, the angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) that degrades bradykinin (Cicardi and Zuraw, 2018; Davin et al., 2019) was downregulated eightfold in COVID-19 BALF.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: ACE was downregulated eightfold in COVID-19 BALF.
source: Furthermore, the angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) that degrades bradykinin (Cicardi and Zuraw, 2018; Davin et al., 2019) was downregulated eightfold in COVID-19 BALF.
evidence: This is a direct finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Tissue factor is the primary initiator of thrombin generation in vivo.
source: The integral cytoplasmic membrane protein tissue factor (TF, encoded by F3) is the primary initiator of thrombin generation in vivo.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the coagulation system.

claim: In many inflammatory conditions, cellular TF expression is upregulated.
source: In many inflammatory conditions, cellular TF expression is upregulated (Edwards et al., 1979), providing a mechanistic explanation for hypercoagulable states associated with a variety of bacterial and viral infections (Grover and Mackman, 2018; Levi and van der Poll, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: TFPI is produced by vascular endothelium.
source: Tissue factor pathway inhibitor (TFPI, encoded by TFPI) is a Kunitz-type protease inhibitor produced by vascular endothelium (Bajaj et al., 1990) and is the major inhibitor of the factor VIIa (FVIIa)/TF complex (Wood et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: TFPI is the major inhibitor of the factor VIIa/TF complex.
source: Tissue factor pathway inhibitor (TFPI, encoded by TFPI) is a Kunitz-type protease inhibitor produced by vascular endothelium (Bajaj et al., 1990) and is the major inhibitor of the factor VIIa (FVIIa)/TF complex (Wood et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Transcripts encoding TF were similar in COVID-19 and control BALF samples.
source: Surprisingly, transcripts encoding TF were similar in COVID-19 and control BALF samples (Figure 1; Table 1), whereas transcripts for TFPI were increased eightfold in COVID-19 BALF.
evidence: This is a direct finding from the study's data analysis, with reference to Figure 1 and Table 1.

claim: Transcripts for TFPI were increased eightfold in COVID-19 BALF.
source: Surprisingly, transcripts encoding TF were similar in COVID-19 and control BALF samples (Figure 1; Table 1), whereas transcripts for TFPI were increased eightfold in COVID-19 BALF.
evidence: This is a direct finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: COVID-19 may dampen TF-dependent mechanisms in the lungs.
source: On balance, these data indicate that pulmonary fibrin deposition does not stem from enhanced local TF production and that counterintuitively, COVID-19 may dampen TF-dependent mechanisms in the lungs.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that TF transcripts are not increased while TFPI is increased.

claim: Pulmonary fibrin deposition in COVID-19 does not stem from enhanced local TF production.
source: On balance, these data indicate that pulmonary fibrin deposition does not stem from enhanced local TF production and that counterintuitively, COVID-19 may dampen TF-dependent mechanisms in the lungs.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that TF transcripts are not increased.

claim: FXIIa does not contribute to hemostasis.
source: While FXIIa does not contribute to hemostasis, it is implicated in thrombo-inflammatory conditions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the coagulation system.

claim: FXIIa is implicated in thrombo-inflammatory conditions.
source: While FXIIa does not contribute to hemostasis, it is implicated in thrombo-inflammatory conditions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the coagulation system.

claim: FXIIa converts factor XI to the protease FXIa.
source: FXIIa converts factor XI (FXI, encoded by F11) to the protease FXIa (Ivanov et al., 2017; Long et al., 2016; Schmaier, 2016; Wang et al., 2019), a potent activator of the coagulation protease factor IX (FIX, encoded by F9) (Mohammed et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: FXIa is a potent activator of factor IX.
source: FXIIa converts factor XI (FXI, encoded by F11) to the protease FXIa (Ivanov et al., 2017; Long et al., 2016; Schmaier, 2016; Wang et al., 2019), a potent activator of the coagulation protease factor IX (FIX, encoded by F9) (Mohammed et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Transcripts encoding FXII were slightly decreased (−4-fold) in COVID-19 BALF samples.
source: Transcripts encoding FXII were slightly decreased (−4-fold) in COVID-19 and control BALF samples (Figure 1; Table 1), but the expression of the C1 inhibitor (encoded by SERPING1), which normally inhibits the FXII protein activity, is downregulated 80-fold.
evidence: This is a direct finding from the study's data analysis, with reference to Figure 1 and Table 1.

claim: C1 inhibitor normally inhibits FXII protein activity.
source: Transcripts encoding FXII were slightly decreased (−4-fold) in COVID-19 and control BALF samples (Figure 1; Table 1), but the expression of the C1 inhibitor (encoded by SERPING1), which normally inhibits the FXII protein activity, is downregulated 80-fold.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the coagulation system.

claim: Transcripts for FXI were increased 81-fold in BALF from COVID-19 patients.
source: While it is not known if pulmonary tissues normally produce FXI or FIX, transcripts for FXI (81-fold) and FIX (190-fold) were both increased in BALF from COVID-19 patients.
evidence: This is a direct finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Transcripts for FIX were increased 190-fold in BALF from COVID-19 patients.
source: While it is not known if pulmonary tissues normally produce FXI or FIX, transcripts for FXI (81-fold) and FIX (190-fold) were both increased in BALF from COVID-19 patients.
evidence: This is a direct finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Numerous studies have reported correlations between plasma FIX and FXI levels and risk for venous thromboembolism and ischemic stroke.
source: Numerous studies have reported correlations between plasma FIX and FXI levels and risk for venous thromboembolism and ischemic stroke (Ammollo et al., 2014; Folsom et al., 2015; Mohammed et al., 2018; Preis et al., 2017; Salomon et al., 2011, Salomon et al., 2008; Siegerink et al., 2010; Suri et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Local increases in FIX or FXI expression may enhance thrombin generation and promote thrombus formation.
source: Perhaps local increases in FIX or FXI expression enhance thrombin generation and promote thrombus formation.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed increases in FIX and FXI transcripts.

claim: Healthy lung endothelium has membrane-associated anticoagulant proteins that inhibit different points in the thrombin generation pathway.
source: Healthy lung endothelium has membrane-associated anticoagulant proteins that inhibit different points in the thrombin generation pathway.
evidence: This is established knowledge about lung endothelium.

claim: Thrombomodulin and EPCR coordinate to inhibit the propagation of coagulation.
source: These include TFPI, which inhibits the initiation of coagulation as described above, and thrombomodulin (encoded by THBD) and endothelial protein C receptor (EPCR, encoded by PROCR), which coordinate to inhibit the propagation of coagulation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the anticoagulant system.

claim: Thrombomodulin captures thrombin and converts it from a procoagulant enzyme to an activator of protein C.
source: Thrombomodulin captures thrombin and converts it from a procoagulant enzyme to an activator of protein C (encoded by PROC) in a process enhanced by binding of PC to EPCR.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the anticoagulant system.

claim: Binding of protein C to EPCR enhances the activation of protein C by thrombomodulin.
source: Thrombomodulin captures thrombin and converts it from a procoagulant enzyme to an activator of protein C (encoded by PROC) in a process enhanced by binding of PC to EPCR.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the anticoagulant system.

claim: Activated protein C with its cofactor protein S downregulates thrombin generation by inactivating factors VIIIa and Va.
source: Activated PC with its cofactor protein S (encoded by PROS1) downregulates thrombin generation by inactivating factors VIIIa and Va and produces a cytoprotective/anti-inflammatory effect when bound to EPCR through cleavage of protease activated receptor-1 on endothelial cells (Ito et al., 2019; Riewald et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Activated protein C produces a cytoprotective/anti-inflammatory effect when bound to EPCR through cleavage of protease activated receptor-1 on endothelial cells.
source: Activated PC with its cofactor protein S (encoded by PROS1) downregulates thrombin generation by inactivating factors VIIIa and Va and produces a cytoprotective/anti-inflammatory effect when bound to EPCR through cleavage of protease activated receptor-1 on endothelial cells (Ito et al., 2019; Riewald et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Transcripts encoding thrombomodulin were reduced 22-fold in BALF from COVID-19 patients compared with controls.
source: Transcripts encoding thrombomodulin (−22-fold) and EPCR (−33-fold) were each reduced in BALF from COVID-19 patients compared with controls (Figure 1; Table 1), suggesting SARS-CoV-2 is associated with reduced expression of these proteins on vascular endothelium.
evidence: This is a direct finding from the study's data analysis, with reference to Figure 1 and Table 1.

claim: Transcripts encoding EPCR were reduced 33-fold in BALF from COVID-19 patients compared with controls.
source: Transcripts encoding thrombomodulin (−22-fold) and EPCR (−33-fold) were each reduced in BALF from COVID-19 patients compared with controls (Figure 1; Table 1), suggesting SARS-CoV-2 is associated with reduced expression of these proteins on vascular endothelium.
evidence: This is a direct finding from the study's data analysis, with reference to Figure 1 and Table 1.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 is associated with reduced expression of thrombomodulin and EPCR on vascular endothelium.
source: Transcripts encoding thrombomodulin (−22-fold) and EPCR (−33-fold) were each reduced in BALF from COVID-19 patients compared with controls (Figure 1; Table 1), suggesting SARS-CoV-2 is associated with reduced expression of these proteins on vascular endothelium.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed reduction in transcripts for these proteins.

claim: There was a marked increase in protein C transcripts in BALF from COVID-19 patients (227-fold).
source: We also observed a marked increase in protein C transcripts in BALF from COVID-19 patients (227-fold), but a significant reduction in PS transcripts (−54-fold).
evidence: This is a direct finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: There was a significant reduction in protein S transcripts (−54-fold) in BALF from COVID-19 patients.
source: We also observed a marked increase in protein C transcripts in BALF from COVID-19 patients (227-fold), but a significant reduction in PS transcripts (−54-fold).
evidence: This is a direct finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Protein C and protein S in blood are primarily synthesized by hepatocytes.
source: Since protein C and protein S in blood are primarily synthesized by hepatocytes, the importance of local synthesis of these proteins is not known.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the source of these proteins.

claim: The plasma concentration of protein C is moderately elevated in COVID-19 patients.
source: However, expression patterns in BALF are consistent with the observation that the plasma concentration of protein C is moderately elevated, and protein S moderately reduced, in COVID-19 patients (Panigada et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a clinical study.

claim: The plasma concentration of protein S is moderately reduced in COVID-19 patients.
source: However, expression patterns in BALF are consistent with the observation that the plasma concentration of protein C is moderately elevated, and protein S moderately reduced, in COVID-19 patients (Panigada et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a clinical study.

claim: There was a substantial increase (786-fold) in mRNA for protein C inhibitor in COVID-19 BALF.
source: In COVID-19 BALF, there was also a substantial increase (786-fold) in mRNA for protein C inhibitor (encoded by SERPINA5), a serpin regulator of activated protein C.
evidence: This is a direct finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Protein C inhibitor is a serpin regulator of activated protein C.
source: In COVID-19 BALF, there was also a substantial increase (786-fold) in mRNA for protein C inhibitor (encoded by SERPINA5), a serpin regulator of activated protein C.
evidence: This is established knowledge about protein C inhibitor.

claim: The transcript pattern in COVID-19 BALF suggests a diminished capacity of the endothelial anticoagulant system to downregulate local thrombin generation.
source: Taken as a whole, the transcript pattern in COVID-19 BALF suggests a diminished capacity of the endothelial anticoagulant system to downregulate local thrombin generation.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined findings of reduced anticoagulant proteins and increased protein C inhibitor.

claim: The fibrinolytic system is responsible for enzymatic degradation of fibrin.
source: The fibrinolytic system is responsible for enzymatic degradation of fibrin.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the fibrinolytic system.

claim: Plasminogen activators convert plasminogen to plasmin.
source: Plasminogen activators convert plasminogen to plasmin, which cleaves fibrin and generates fibrin degradation products, including the circulating biomarker D-dimer.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the fibrinolytic system.

claim: Plasmin cleaves fibrin and generates fibrin degradation products, including D-dimer.
source: Plasminogen activators convert plasminogen to plasmin, which cleaves fibrin and generates fibrin degradation products, including the circulating biomarker D-dimer.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the fibrinolytic system.

claim: Cells within the lung express plasminogen activators that prevent fibrin accumulation in small airways and the alveolar compartment.
source: Cells within the lung express plasminogen activators (e.g., [tPA, encoded by PLAT], urokinase plasminogen activator [uPA, encoded by PLAU], and the uPA receptor [uPAR, encoded by PLAUR]) that prevent fibrin accumulation in small airways and the alveolar compartment and that maintain blood vessel patency (Shetty et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Lung plasminogen activators maintain blood vessel patency.
source: Cells within the lung express plasminogen activators (e.g., [tPA, encoded by PLAT], urokinase plasminogen activator [uPA, encoded by PLAU], and the uPA receptor [uPAR, encoded by PLAUR]) that prevent fibrin accumulation in small airways and the alveolar compartment and that maintain blood vessel patency (Shetty et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: uPA and uPAR are expressed by lung epithelial cells, alveolar macrophages, and fibroblasts.
source: uPA and uPAR are expressed by lung epithelial cells, alveolar macrophages, and fibroblasts, and reduced expression of these proteins contributes to acute lung injury (Shetty et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Reduced expression of uPA and uPAR contributes to acute lung injury.
source: uPA and uPAR are expressed by lung epithelial cells, alveolar macrophages, and fibroblasts, and reduced expression of these proteins contributes to acute lung injury (Shetty et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Plasminogen activators are inhibited by plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1).
source: The plasminogen activators are inhibited by plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1, encoded by SERPINE1).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the fibrinolytic system.

claim: Plasma fibrinogen is synthesized primarily by hepatocytes.
source: Plasma fibrinogen, a dimer of trimers (Aα2Bβ2γ2) encoded by three genes, FGA, FGB, and FGG, is synthesized primarily by hepatocytes (Pieters and Wolberg, 2019); however, synthesis has been reported in stimulated cultured lung alveolar epithelial cells and in alveolar epithelium in an animal model of bacterial pneumonia (Guadiz et al., 1997; Simpson-Haidaris et al., 1998).

claim: Fibrinogen synthesis has been reported in stimulated cultured lung alveolar epithelial cells.
